segments.text: Think about a person you really trust at work.
When they say they'll do something, you believe them.
You can speak openly with them. You don't waste time second-guessing their
intentions. And when something goes wrong, you know you can have an honest
conversation and move forward. Now imagine the opposite.
Information gets withheld. Promises are made but not kept.
Mistakes get hidden. People start checking up on each other, protecting themselves,
and questioning motives. Everything slows down.
This is one of the central ideas in Stephen M.R.
Covey's "The Speed of Trust." When trust goes up, speed goes up, and cost
goes down. When trust goes down, speed goes down, and cost goes up.
Covey describes this as the difference between a trust dividend and a trust tax.
In a high-trust environment, communication is faster, decisions are easier, people
collaborate more freely, problems are raised earlier.
But low-trust organizations pay a tax, more meetings, more checking, more
misunderstandings, more delays, and more stress.
Trust isn't simply a nice value to put on the wall.
It has a practical and economic impact, and every one of us contributes to it.
So how do we build more trust? Here are six behaviors we can start practicing
immediately. Number one, talk straight. Say what you mean.
Be honest about problems. Have the conversations that need to be had.
Talking straight doesn't mean being aggressive or insensitive.
It means being clear, respectful, and truthful.
Instead of allowing frustration to build, say, "I think we may have a problem here.
Can we talk about it?" A short, honest conversation today can prevent a much larger
problem tomorrow. Number two, create clarity.
A surprising amount of conflict comes from unclear expectations.
One person thinks success means one thing.
Another thinks it means something completely different.
Before important work begins, get clear. What are we trying to achieve?
Who is responsible for what? When does it need to happen?
And what does a successful result look like? Clarity builds confidence.
Ambiguity creates distrust. Number three, keep commitments.
Trust is built when our words and actions match.
If you say you are going to do something, do everything you reasonably can to
follow through. Sometimes circumstances change.
The important thing is to communicate early.
If you can no longer deliver what you promised, say, "Something has changed.
Here's the situation, and here's what I propose we do." Trust does not require
perfection. It requires integrity. Number four, practice accountability.
When something goes wrong, low-trust cultures ask, "Who can we blame?" High-trust
cultures ask, "What happened? What can we learn?
And how do we fix it?" If you made the mistake, own it.
Imagine someone simply saying, "That was my responsibility. I got it wrong.
Here's what I'm doing to correct it."
Taking responsibility doesn't weaken credibility. Very often, it strengthens it.
Number five, listen first. Many trust problems begin with assumptions.
We assume we know why someone behaved a certain way. We assume they don't care.
We assume they had bad intentions. But assumptions are not facts.
Instead, become curious. Ask, "Help me understand what
happened." Listen before defending. Understand before judging.
People are far more likely to trust us when they feel genuinely heard.
Number six, extend trust. Trust also has to be given.
If capable people are constantly monitored and second-guessed, eventually they stop
taking initiative. Strong leaders give people appropriate responsibility and allow
them to own the result. That doesn't mean blind trust.
It means what Covey describes as smart trust. Consider the situation.
Consider the person's competence and character. Then give them enough trust to act.
Responsibility grows when people are trusted with responsibility.
So here is a simple challenge. During the next week, pay attention to the trust you
create around you. Ask yourself, "Do I speak honestly?
Do I make expectations clear? Do I keep my commitments?
Do I take responsibility for my mistakes? Do I genuinely listen?
And do I give trustworthy people the opportunity to take ownership?" Trust is not
created by one big event. It is created through hundreds of small moments.
A promise kept, a difficult truth spoken respectfully, a mistake acknowledged,
a person listened to, a responsibility entrusted.
Over time, those moments create something extremely valuable.
A team where people can move quickly because they don't have to protect themselves
from one another. A team where communication becomes easier, where accountability
becomes normal, and where more energy can be spent doing great work.
So if you want better communication, stronger teamwork, and better performance,
start with trust. Because when trust increases, almost everything else becomes
easier.
